summary: Describes a family of tests receiving mail servers can use to check whether an email address was used with the permission of the owner of the domain. It was meant to fight spoofed addresses. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Sender ID lets a receiving mail system check whether the server sending a message is authorized by the sender's domain. It looks up domain policy in DNS, but checks only the domain, not the part of the address before the at sign.

questions: how to stop spoofed email addresses
how does sender id prevent email spoofing
what are the security limitations of sender id
how does sender id check a domain
subtitle: A DNS-based test of whether a mail server is authorized to send for an email domain.

tldr.problem: Email can use sender addresses without the domain owner's permission, so a receiving system needs a way to check the sending server.
tldr.mechanism: Sender ID checks either the Purported Responsible Address or the SMTP MAIL FROM address against SPF information published in DNS.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4406 is Historic. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

today: RFC 4406 is Historic. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What Sender ID Checks
sections.content:
Sender ID describes tests that a receiving mail system can use to check whether an SMTP client has permission to send on behalf of a mailbox's domain. It defines checks for the Purported Responsible Address (PRA) and the Reverse-Path, also called the MAIL FROM address.

The check authenticates the domain associated with the address. It does not authenticate the local part of the address, and the RFC leaves the receiver to decide what action to take based on the result.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiving system checks whether the sending server is allowed by the address's domain. It does not confirm that the specific mailbox name before the at sign is valid.

sections.title: SPF Records and Check Scope
sections.content:
A domain publishes information about its authorized outgoing mail servers in DNS. Sender ID defines the spf2.0 record form and lets the domain state whether a record applies to the mfrom scope, the pra scope or both.

The MAIL FROM check concerns the address that receives delivery-status notifications. The PRA check concerns the address identified as responsible for the message under the rules in RFC 4407. The RFC permits older v=spf1 records to be used for both scopes when no matching SPF 2.0 record exists.
sections.plainLanguage: A domain publishes which servers may send its mail. Sender ID has separate checks for the bounce address and for the address identified as responsible for the message.

sections.title: How the Receiver Gets a Result
sections.content:
The receiver extracts the address for the selected scope, gets its domain and calls the SPF check with the scope, sending IP address, domain and address. The check returns one of seven results: Pass, Fail, SoftFail, Neutral, None, TempError or PermError.

The RFC does not require a single action for every result. For example, an SMTP server should not reject a message solely because the result is Neutral, None, SoftFail or PermError, though it may use other checks. A Pass means the message should be treated as authentic, subject to other policies.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver finds the relevant address and its domain, then checks the sending server against the domain's DNS policy. The result guides the receiver, but the RFC does not make every result an automatic accept or reject decision.

sections.title: Changes for Mail Senders and Relays
sections.content:
Domains that send original mail should publish authorization information in DNS. A forwarder or mailing-list server that wants its outgoing message to pass the checks must use an address it controls for MAIL FROM and add an appropriate header for the PRA check.

The RFC also advises mail user agents to show the verified address when it differs from the From address. This helps readers see which address the check actually covered.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail services that forward or redistribute a message may need to identify themselves in its headers and return address. A mail program should show the checked address if it differs from the visible From address.

sections.title: Limits and Attacks
sections.content:
Sender ID depends on DNS, so forged DNS replies can affect its result. The RFC also discusses forged TCP source addresses, altered IP routing and message headers that cause the check to validate a different address from the visible From address.

These checks do not prevent every form of mail forgery. The RFC recommends that mail programs display the address that was checked and notes that receivers may apply additional security measures.
sections.plainLanguage: The check trusts DNS and the address-selection rules, so an attacker may still mislead it. Sender ID can help identify unauthorized sending, but it does not prove that every part of a message is genuine.

references.text: Lyon, J., "Purported Responsible Address in E-Mail Messages", RFC 4407, April 2006.
